candidates.raw_excerpt: The recent HAPS flight of a Sceye vehicle also included a laser tracking demonstration. Sceye and Softbank conducted the demonstration in August, flying a Sceye HAPS from New Mexico to Japan and back, demonstrating mobile broadband connectivity and edge computing. The ground-based equipment included a portable laser ranging system based on “Omni-SLR” designed by Hitotsubashi University. The ST1 HAPS mission lasted from Aug. 9 through Sept. 5 as the first flight in Sceye’s Service Test program. The AI’s proof could help the field after “some serious re-writing,” he added, but “as of today, the paper doesn’t teach us much.” The Navier-Stokes equations mathematically describe how fluids, ranging from a rush of wind to the churn of ocean currents, move and behave. candidates.raw_excerpt: Planet officially opened its new Berlin manufacturing facility on Tuesday, marking facility handover and cleanroom fit-out. The 5,700-square-meter facility, announced last year to double Pelican satellite production capacity, is expected to begin production this fall. It’s a key part of Planet’s expansion in Germany, which has been the company’s base in Europe for 10 years. Planet aims to meet growing demand from the European market and hire 70 new employees in addition to the company’s 150 employees in Berlin already. “When you couple [Planet] being there for a decade [with] the largest economy in Europe, needing to re-industrialize the space ecosystem, the tech talent there is phenomena in optics, signals processing, and Earth Observation — that it was the natural step for us to just expand that office and add a factory,” Planet co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer Robbie Schingler told Via Satellite last week during World Space Business Week. Ahead of the factory opening, Planet recently signed a deal to launch the first Pelican satellite built in Germany with Isar Aerospace on a German-built rocket. The launch itself will take place from the Andøya Space complex in Norway. Isar Aerospace just had success with its second launch, another piece of momentum for Germany’s space industry. The Planet/Isar launch is expected in early 2027. Planet has longstanding German customers and partners including the German Federal Agency for Cartography and Geodesy (BKG). Schingler noted that Planet looks to support Spock-2, a Bundeswehr planned multi-sensor imaging and sensing satellite constellation. “We hope to be central to the coalition to support Germany to have their own eyes, and to be able to also serve other European customers that want much more of a European space ecosystem, so that they could they could choose to purchase satellites from our German factory,” Schingler added. candidates.raw_excerpt: TRL11 has received a NASA contract to provide imaging systems for the Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom mission to Mars. “It will be the first time a camera we built travels to another planet and captures images of it,” TRL11 CEO Nicolaas Verheem said in a statement.  Freedom isn’t free: The $2B SR-1 mission is expected to launch in late 2028 to Mars as the first fission-powered interplanetary spacecraft. NASA first announced SR-1 at the space agency’s Ignition event in March. In addition to demoing how nuclear tech can help with interplanetary deep space travel, SR-1 will deliver a trio of SkyFall helicopters to Mars to conduct advance work for future crewed missions to the red planet. What’s onboard: TRL11 will build space cameras and edge computing systems for SR-1, according to a press release. That hardware will enable NASA to capture, process, and store high-res imagery of the mission—including the moment SkyFall deploys to Mars—and ensure the photos can be sent back to Earth. NASA is also considering adding more of TRL11’s tech to the mission, according to a press release, including: VIPLink comms system; VIP1st software to prioritize downloads; Commander software to manage spacecraft imaging. Teamwork makes the dream work: TRL11 isn’t the only company contributing to the Martian mission. AeroVironment is co-designing and co-manufacturing the SkyFall helos, in partnership with JPL. Firefly Aerospace won a $13M contract to build the landing aeroshell, ensuring that SkyFall doesn’t become a fireball after its long flight.
